newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs attack the Hague over rice sector crisis.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs attack the Hague over rice sector crisis.

text.p: The European Parliament lashed out at the Netherlands on Friday for blocking changes in European Union rice import rules which Euro-MPs said were essential to end the crisis in the EU rice market.

A 1991 agreement which allows the EU's overseas countries and territories (OCTs) in the Caribbean to export rice to the EU free of duty was "a root cause of this serious crisis", Euro-MPs said in a resolution.
But the Hague's "obstructive attitude" was preventing a revision of the 1991 agreement, Euro-MPs said.
As a result of the 1991 concessions, total exports from OCTs rose from 58,000 to 192,000 tonnes between 1992 and 1995 and reached 365,029 tonnes in 1996.
Much of the growth has come from the Dutch West Indies -- Curacao, Bonaire and Aruba -- the European Commission says.
The Commission and all EU member states bar the Netherlands agree these low price imports are undermining the EU's domestic rice production and the 1991 decision must therefore be changed.
Concessions for OCT sugar are also disrupting the EU market.
But the OCT agreement, which does not expire until the year 2000, cannot be altered without the approval of all EU states.

The deadlock and the subsequent crisis in the domestic rice market led the EU in January, at the behest of rice growers Italy and Spain, to introduce safeguard measures strictly limiting OCT duty free imports between January and April.
The continued slump in Community rice prices caused the Commission on April 9 to propose extending the safeguard clause for another four months, a decision welcomed by the parliament.
The impasse is increasingly worrying Paris and London because new EU financing for their Caribbean territories cannot be released until the OCT agreement has been revised.
French and British diplomats also say they fear other member states are so annoyed they will not agree to renew the OCT decision in 2000.
The parliament's resolution also attacked a proposed new Cumulative Recovery System (CRS) for rice imports, saying the EU was submitting to blackmail from the United States.

The optional CRS would allow traders from the U.S., Egypt and other third countries to recover excess EU import duty payments if they can prove that these are higher than levels set under the GATT Uruguay Round agreement.
The proposed CRS led to the U.S. withdrawing last month a complaint to the World Trade Organisation.
